title: Neurons and Neurotransmitters
body:
## What it is
The nervous system controls movement, sensation, autonomic function, thinking and behavior. The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is the cranial nerves, spinal nerves and the autonomic nervous system.

## Must-know facts
- The neuron is the basic working unit. Dendrites carry impulses toward the cell body; the axon carries them away.
- Sensory (afferent) neurons carry impulses from receptors to the CNS. Motor (efferent) neurons carry impulses from the CNS to effectors such as muscles and glands. Interneurons stay inside the CNS and link sensory and motor pathways.
- Neurotransmitters pass messages from one neuron to another or to a target tissue. They can excite or inhibit.

## Neurotransmitters at a glance
- Dopamine: excitatory in the handout; complex movement, motivation, cognition, emotional response. Low in Parkinson's disease.
- Norepinephrine: excitatory; attention, learning, memory, sleep-wake, mood.
- Epinephrine: excitatory; fight-or-flight.
- Serotonin: inhibitory; fluid intake, sleep, temperature, pain control, sexual behavior, emotion.
- Acetylcholine: excitatory or inhibitory; sleep-wake cycle, makes muscles alert. Low in myasthenia gravis and Alzheimer's disease.
- GABA: inhibitory; calms and modulates other transmitters.
- Glutamate: excitatory; too much is toxic to neurons (linked to ALS).

## How the exam asks about it
Questions usually link a transmitter to a disease: dopamine to Parkinson's, acetylcholine to myasthenia gravis and Alzheimer's, glutamate to ALS. Learn the pairing, then the drug that corrects it.

## Related topics
[[Parkinson's Disease: Signs and Pathophysiology]], [[Myasthenia Gravis]], [[Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis]], [[Brain Regions and Their Functions]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout writes "glutamine"; the excitatory transmitter meant here is glutamate.
- Labeling dopamine as purely excitatory is a simplification; its effect depends on the receptor.

title: Brain Regions and Their Functions
body:
## What it is
Knowing which region does what lets you predict the deficit from the site of injury, a common exam style.

## Cerebrum (four lobes)
- Frontal: the largest lobe. Concentration, abstract thought, memory storage, and generation of voluntary movement. Holds Broca's area (motor control of speech).
- Parietal: sensory function: touch, taste, temperature. This is where sensations are felt.
- Temporal: hearing and smell; memory of sound, understanding of language and music. Holds Wernicke's area (language comprehension).
- Occipital: visual interpretation and visual memory.

## Brain stem and others
- Cerebellum: fine movement, balance, position sense (proprioception).
- Medulla: cardiac, respiratory and vasomotor centers, plus reflex centers for coughing, sneezing, swallowing and vomiting. Damage here is life threatening.
- Pons: sits in front of the cerebellum and above the medulla; contains the apneustic and pneumotaxic respiratory centers that set a normal breathing rhythm.
- Midbrain: visual, auditory and righting reflexes.
- Hypothalamus: hormone production, body temperature, food and fluid intake, and coordination of the autonomic nervous system.
- Thalamus: relays sensation and can suppress minor sensations.

## How the exam asks about it
- Expressive aphasia points to Broca's area (frontal); receptive aphasia points to Wernicke's area (temporal).
- Visual field loss after a stroke points to the occipital pathway.
- Priority thinking: medulla and pons control breathing and heart rate, so injury there threatens airway and circulation first.

## Memory aid
Broca = "broken speech" (can't produce words); Wernicke = "can't understand". Made-up helper.

## Related topics
[[Stroke: Deficits and Left versus Right Hemisphere]], [[Increased Intracranial Pressure]], [[Neurons and Neurotransmitters]]
outlineRefs: Cerebrum: frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital lobes

title: Cranial Nerves: Names, Types and Functions
body:
## What it is
Twelve pairs of nerves from the brain. Each is sensory (S), motor (M) or mixed (B for both).

## The twelve
- I Olfactory (S): smell.
- II Optic (S): vision and visual acuity.
- III Oculomotor (M): most eye movement, lifting the eyelid, pupil constriction, lens accommodation.
- IV Trochlear (M): eye movement (downward and inward gaze; the handout tests upward movement).
- V Trigeminal (B): facial sensation, corneal reflex, chewing.
- VI Abducens (M): eye movement (outward).
- VII Facial (B): facial expression, tearing and salivation, taste on the front of the tongue, ear sensation.
- VIII Vestibulocochlear (S): hearing and balance.
- IX Glossopharyngeal (B): taste (back of tongue), throat sensation, pharyngeal muscles, swallowing.
- X Vagus (B): muscles of pharynx, larynx and soft palate; sensation of ear, throat and organs; parasympathetic supply to chest and abdominal organs.
- XI Spinal accessory (M): sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (turn head, shrug).
- XII Hypoglossal (M): tongue movement.

## Memory aid
"Some Say Marry Money, But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter More" gives S, S, M, M, B, M, B, S, B, B, M, M. Widely used, not from the handout.

## How the exam asks about it
Match a finding to a nerve: dysphagia to IX or X, facial droop to VII, cannot shrug to XI, tongue deviates to XII, double vision to III/IV/VI.

## Related topics
[[Cranial Nerve Testing and Deficits]], [[Bell's Palsy]], [[Trigeminal Neuralgia]]

## Check against your textbook
Verify the detailed actions of IV (usually described as downward gaze) and the taste territory of VII versus IX.
outlineRefs: Peripheral Nervous System: Cranial Nerves table

title: Cranial Nerve Testing and Deficits
body:
## What it is
Bedside tests for each cranial nerve and the problem a failed test suggests.

## Test and finding, nerve by nerve
- I: eyes closed, identify a familiar smell (coffee, cinnamon), one nostril at a time. Problem: anosmia.
- II: Snellen chart, visual fields, ophthalmoscope. Problem: hemianopia, poor acuity, blindness.
- III: eye movement toward the nose, conjugate gaze, pupil size and light reaction, lid opening. Problem: dysconjugate gaze, double vision, dilated pupil with or without poor light reaction.
- IV and VI: follow the examiner's finger through the gaze directions. Problem: dysconjugate gaze, gaze weakness, double vision.
- V: eyes closed, identify touch on face (three branches); touch a cotton wisp to the cornea (normal: blink and tearing); clench the jaw and palpate muscles. Problem: absent corneal reflex, facial numbness, jaw weakness.
- VII: frown, smile, wrinkle forehead, check symmetry. Problem: facial weakness, cannot close eyelid, taste loss.
- VIII: whisper or watch-tick test, Weber, Rinne, Romberg (balance with eyes closed). Problem: hearing loss, poor balance.
- IX: swallowing and sugar-versus-salt taste on the back third of the tongue. Problem: dysphagia, taste change.
- X: gag reflex, hoarseness, say "ah" and watch the uvula and soft palate rise evenly. Problem: weak gag, dysarthria, hoarseness.
- XI: turn head and shrug against resistance. Problem: weak shrug, cannot turn head.
- XII: stick out and move the tongue. Problem: swallowing trouble, slurred speech.

## Priority nursing actions
Before feeding a client with an absent gag reflex, stop and report: aspiration risk affects airway, the first priority.

## Related topics
[[Cranial Nerves: Names, Types and Functions]], [[Hearing Tests: Weber, Rinne and Audiometry]], [[Stroke: Nursing Management]]
outlineRefs: Cranial Nerves I to XII assessment

title: Spinal Nerves and the Autonomic Nervous System
body:
## What it is
Spinal nerves: 31 pairs: cervical 8, thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacral 5, coccygeal 1. The autonomic nervous system (ANS) regulates organ activity to keep internal balance (homeostasis).

## Two divisions
- Sympathetic: fight or flight.
- Parasympathetic: dominates when relaxed and not stressed ("rest and digest").

## Effects compared (parasympathetic versus sympathetic)
- Pupils: constricted versus dilated.
- Heart rate: decreased versus increased; blood pressure decreased versus increased.
- Coronary vessels: constricted versus dilated. Skeletal muscle vessels dilate with sympathetic. Skin and abdominal vessels constrict with sympathetic.
- Bronchioles: constricted versus dilated; breathing rate decreased versus increased.
- Gut movement: increased versus decreased; sphincters relax versus contract; digestive secretions increased versus little effect.
- Saliva: thin and watery versus thick and sticky.
- Liver: sympathetic raises glucose release from glycogen.
- Bladder wall: contracts (parasympathetic) versus relaxes (sympathetic); sphincters relax versus contract.
- Sympathetic only: sweating, goose bumps, adrenal medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine.

## How the exam asks about it
Predict effects of a drug or injury: anticholinergics block parasympathetic action, so expect dry mouth, urinary retention, dilated pupils, fast heart rate. Loss of sympathetic control above T6 is behind [[Autonomic Dysreflexia]].

## Memory aid
Parasympathetic = "slow and digest"; sympathetic = "fight, flight, dilate lungs and pupils, speed the heart". Made-up helper.

## Related topics
[[Spinal Cord Injury]], [[Neurons and Neurotransmitters]], [[Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma]]

title: Level of Consciousness and Glasgow Coma Scale
body:
## What it is
Neurologic assessment covers cerebral function (level of consciousness and mental status), cranial nerves (motor and sensory) and reflexes. Level of consciousness (LOC) is the most sensitive early sign of neurologic change.

## Assessing cerebral function
- Judge alertness and how strong a stimulus is needed to get a response.
- Orientation: ask person, place and time.
- Use a painful stimulus on the nail bed with a blunt object when needed.

## Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
Three areas are scored:
- Eye opening (1 to 4): spontaneous 4, to sound 3, to pressure 2, none 1.
- Verbal (1 to 5): oriented 5, confused 4, words 3, sounds 2, none 1.
- Motor (1 to 6): obeys 6, localizes pain 5, withdraws 4, abnormal flexion (decorticate) 3, abnormal extension (decerebrate) 2, none 1.
- Highest score 15 (alert and oriented). Lowest 3 (deep coma). The handout calls a score below 7 comatose.
- Updated GCS-P (2015) adds pupil reactivity: both pupils unreactive 2, one 1, neither 0; subtract this from the GCS total.

## Priority nursing actions
Trend scores over time: a falling total means worsening. Report a drop at once; an unwatched drop can mean rising pressure in the skull.

## Related topics
[[Increased Intracranial Pressure]], [[Meningeal Signs, Babinski and Posturing]], [[Disability and Exposure in the Primary Survey]]

## Check against your textbook
Many sources use 8 or less as the coma cut-off, not below 7. Confirm the cut-off your school teaches.

title: Meningeal Signs, Babinski and Posturing
body:
## What it is
Abnormal reflexes and postures that point to meningeal irritation or serious brain damage.

## Meningeal irritation
- Brudzinski sign: client supine, nurse flexes the head toward the chest. Positive when pain and resistance occur and the hips and knees flex on their own.
- Kernig sign: client supine with hips and knees flexed; extending the knee causes pain or resistance. Positive means meningeal irritation.
- Both signs are seen in [[Meningitis]].

## Babinski reflex
Stroke the outer edge of the sole. Normal in adults: toes curl down and draw together. Abnormal (positive): toes fan out and the big toe goes up. This points to an upper motor neuron problem. (A fanning response is normal in infants.)

## Posturing
- Decorticate: arms pulled in, elbows, wrists and fingers flexed, legs extended and turned in, feet fixed. Lesion at or above the upper brain stem.
- Decerebrate: arms and legs extended, arms turned in. More dangerous; lower brain-stem damage.
- A change from decorticate to decerebrate means worsening injury.

## Priority nursing actions
Report new posturing immediately; check airway, breathing and pupils, then GCS.

## Memory aid
Decorticate = "toward the core" (flexed in); decerebrate = "extended out". Made-up helper.

## Related topics
[[Level of Consciousness and Glasgow Coma Scale]], [[Increased Intracranial Pressure]]

## Check against your textbook
The infant Babinski note is added from general knowledge.

title: Neurologic Diagnostic Tests and Nursing Care
body:
## What it is
Imaging and recording tests used to find brain and spinal disorders.

## Tests
- Skull and spine X-ray: shows fracture, dislocation, compression. Care: support a confused or combative client, remove metal items, keep the spine immobilized.
- CT scan: finds hemorrhage, brain shrinkage, tumors, skull fractures, abscesses. Care: ask about iodine allergy (if contrast is used), explain to lie still on a moving table, warn of a hot flush and metallic taste, remove hairpins and metal.
- MRI: good for degenerative disease and intracranial or spinal abnormalities; not helpful for bone problems. Safety point: remove all metal (ask about pacemakers and implants).
- EEG: records brain electrical activity through scalp electrodes. Care: withhold drugs that interfere (anticonvulsants, sedatives, stimulants) as ordered; adults sleep no more than 5 hours the night before.
- Cerebral angiography: dye injected into the carotid, vertebral, femoral or brachial artery, then X-ray; shows tumors, aneurysm, blocked vessels, hematomas, abscesses.

## Priority nursing actions
Before any dye test: allergy check first (anaphylaxis risk). After angiography: check the puncture site, distal pulses and neurologic status (standard practice, not in the handout).

## Related topics
[[Stroke: Types, Causes and Risk Factors]], [[Seizure Types and Epilepsy]], [[Increased Intracranial Pressure]]

## Check against your textbook
- Pacemaker and implant safety for MRI and post-angiography checks are added from general knowledge.
- Ask whether your instructor wants the EEG medication-hold rule stated as "per order".

title: Headache Types and Migraine Phases
body:
## What it is
Headache (cephalgia) is a symptom, not a disease. Primary headaches have no organic cause; secondary headaches come from a cause such as a tumor or aneurysm.

## Primary headaches
- Migraine: repeated attacks of severe throbbing, pounding pain lasting 4 to 72 hours in adults. Classic migraine has a pre-headache aura (vision change, speech difficulty, numbness or tingling). Common migraine has no aura.
- Tension-type: the most common; chronic and less severe; pressure or tight feeling in the temple area.
- Cluster: severe vascular headache; more common in men.

## Four phases of migraine
- Prodrome (hours to days before): depression, irritability, feeling cold, loss of appetite, activity change, more urination, diarrhea or constipation.
- Aura (less than 1 hour): flashes and bright spots, numbness or tingling of lips, face or hands, mild confusion, slight weakness, drowsiness, dizziness.
- Headache (hours, up to 4 to 72 hours): throbbing pain, light sensitivity, nausea and vomiting.
- Recovery (postdrome): pain fades, neck muscle contraction, tenderness, exhaustion.

## How the exam asks about it
Spot a "worst headache of life" or a new headache with neurologic signs as secondary (possible bleed), not migraine: that is the safety-first answer.

## Related topics
[[Migraine Drugs and Headache Nursing Care]], [[Increased Intracranial Pressure]], [[Stroke: Types, Causes and Risk Factors]]

title: Migraine Drugs and Headache Nursing Care
body:
## What it is
Drug approaches and comfort care for migraine and other headaches.

## Two drug approaches
- Abortive: stops or limits a headache at onset or while it is happening. Best for people with infrequent attacks.
- Preventive: for frequent attacks at regular or predictable intervals, or when a medical condition rules out abortive drugs.

## Triptans
- Sumatriptan is the most widely used; works in acute migraine and cluster headache. Others in the class: naratriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan, almotriptan.
- They narrow blood vessels, reduce inflammation and may lessen pain signaling.
- Contraindicated in ischemic heart disease because they can cause chest pain. Ask about heart disease before giving.

## Nursing care
- Goals: relieve pain, treat the acute attack, prevent repeat attacks.
- Quiet, dark room; head of bed raised to 30 degrees; local heat or massage; analgesics as ordered.
- Stress reduction, biofeedback, exercise and meditation give a sense of control.

## Related topics
[[Headache Types and Migraine Phases]], [[Cranial Nerves: Names, Types and Functions]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout lists ondansetron, granisetron and dolasetron as "serotonin receptor agonists" for migraine. These are serotonin (5-HT3) antagonists used as anti-nausea drugs; verify the classification. Preventive drug names are not given in the handout.

title: Increased Intracranial Pressure
body:
## What it is
Rise in pressure inside the skull because brain tissue, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or blood increases in bulk. Normal is 0 to 10 mm Hg; 15 mm Hg is the upper limit.

## Causes
Brain abscess, hemorrhage, edema (swelling), hydrocephalus.

## Findings
- Early: change in level of consciousness (earliest sign), pupil changes (slow or fixed), slowed speech, restlessness, confusion, increasing drowsiness.
- Late: decorticate then decerebrate posturing.
- Cushing's triad: bradycardia, hypertension, bradypnea. A late, ominous sign of herniation.

## Complications
Brain-stem herniation, diabetes insipidus, SIADH.

## Priority nursing actions (and why)
- Airway first: keep it patent; oxygen as ordered. Low oxygen and high carbon dioxide raise pressure.
- Raise head of bed about 30 degrees (unless contraindicated) with head midline so veins drain.
- Prevent Valsalva and other pressure-raising activities (straining, coughing, neck flexion).
- Drugs: mannitol (osmotic diuretic), corticosteroids, anticonvulsants. Medical goals: reduce cerebral edema, lower CSF volume (CSF drainage).
- Tests: CT and MRI most common, angiography, PET.

## How the exam asks about it
"What is the earliest sign?" Answer: change in level of consciousness. "Which finding means herniation?" Cushing's triad.

## Related topics
[[Level of Consciousness and Glasgow Coma Scale]], [[Meningeal Signs, Babinski and Posturing]], [[Stroke: Nursing Management]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's head-of-bed range is garbled ("30 to -15"); 30 degrees is the usual value. Cushing's triad is often described with a widened pulse pressure. The handout says 100% oxygen: confirm your protocol.

title: Stroke: Types, Causes and Risk Factors
body:
## What it is
A stroke (cerebrovascular accident) is a loss of brain function when the blood supply to the brain is cut off. A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a sudden motor or sensory loss that lasts less than 1 hour and clears; it is a warning of a coming stroke.

## Ischemic stroke (blocked vessel)
Usually a thrombus (commonest) or embolus.
- Large artery thrombotic: plaque in large brain vessels.
- Small penetrating artery thrombotic: the most common ischemic type.
- Cardiogenic embolic: linked to dysrhythmia, usually atrial fibrillation.
- Cryptogenic: cause unknown.

## Hemorrhagic stroke (bleeding)
Most often from hypertension.
- Intracerebral hemorrhage: hypertension and cerebral atherosclerosis.
- Intracranial aneurysm: weak, ballooned arterial wall.
- Arteriovenous malformation (AVM): tangle of arteries and veins without a capillary bed, from development.
- Subarachnoid hemorrhage: usually a leaking aneurysm near the Circle of Willis or an AVM.

## Risk factors
Hypertension (major), atrial fibrillation, high lipids, diabetes, age over 55, smoking, carotid stenosis, obesity, heavy alcohol. Handout also lists African-American race.

## Diagnosis
CT scan (first, to tell bleed from clot), MRI, angiography.

## Treatment (general)
Clot-dissolving (thrombolytic) therapy, platelet-inhibiting drugs; carotid endarterectomy for TIA or mild stroke; carotid stenting for severe stenosis.

## Related topics
[[Stroke: Deficits and Left versus Right Hemisphere]], [[Stroke: Nursing Management]], [[Neurologic Diagnostic Tests and Nursing Care]]

## Check against your textbook
Clot-dissolving drugs are only for ischemic stroke after CT rules out bleeding, within a strict time window; the handout gives no window, so check yours.

title: Stroke: Deficits and Left versus Right Hemisphere
body:
## What it is
Deficits depend on which brain area loses blood supply.

## Types of deficits
- Cognitive: confusion, altered level of consciousness.
- Visual: homonymous hemianopsia (half the visual field lost in each eye), loss of peripheral vision, double vision.
- Motor: hemiplegia (most common), hemiparesis, reduced deep tendon reflexes, ataxia.
- Communication: dysarthria (hard to articulate), dysphasia (impaired language), apraxia (cannot do a learned action).
- Sensory: paresthesia.
- Emotional: lability, low stress tolerance, depression, withdrawal, fear, anger, isolation.

## Aphasia
- Expressive: understands but cannot form understandable words; may use single words.
- Receptive: cannot understand speech; speaks but may not make sense.
- Global: both.

## Left versus right hemisphere
- Left stroke: right-sided weakness, right visual field loss, aphasia, altered intellect, slow and cautious behavior.
- Right stroke: left-sided weakness, left visual field loss, spatial-perceptual problems, distractibility, impulsive and poor judgment, unaware of deficits.

## How the exam asks about it
Remember the crossover: brain side opposite to body side. Right-brain patients are the higher fall risk because they are impulsive and unaware of deficits; left-brain patients need communication strategies.

## Memory aid
Left brain = Language (aphasia); right brain = Reckless. Made-up helper.

## Related topics
[[Brain Regions and Their Functions]], [[Stroke: Nursing Management]], [[Stroke: Types, Causes and Risk Factors]]
outlineRefs: Comparison of Left & Right Hemispheric Strokes

title: Stroke: Nursing Management
body:
## What it is
Care after stroke follows priorities: airway and breathing, neurologic monitoring, safety, then rehabilitation.

## Priority nursing actions
- Keep the airway patent. Handout gives 100% oxygen to help lower intracranial pressure.
- Quiet, restful room; monitor vital signs, GCS and pupil size.
- Positioning: lateral initially, then low Fowler's with neck aligned once stable (per handout). Prevent shoulder adduction.

## Hemianopsia safety
- Approach from, and place food and belongings on, the unaffected (seeing) side.
- Teach and remind the client to turn the head toward the blind side to scan.

## Dysphagia (aspiration risk)
- Check the gag reflex before feeding.
- Calm, unhurried; upright position; place food on the unaffected side of the mouth; soft foods; mouth care before and after meals.

## Motor deficits
Keep needed objects within reach on the unaffected side; strengthen the unaffected side; range-of-motion for the affected side; keep body in functional alignment.

## Verbal deficits
Speak slowly and clearly in short sentences; use gestures or pictures; try reading, writing and repeating alphabet sounds.

## Cognitive deficits
Reorient often to time, place and situation; keep familiar objects.

## Related topics
[[Stroke: Deficits and Left versus Right Hemisphere]], [[Increased Intracranial Pressure]], [[Cranial Nerve Testing and Deficits]]

## Check against your textbook
Current guidance gives oxygen only if oxygen saturation is low, and usually raises the head of bed for pressure; the handout's wording conflicts. Follow your school's reference.

title: Meningitis
body:
## What it is
Inflammation of the covering (meninges) of the brain and spinal cord. Causes: bacteria (Neisseria meningitidis), viruses, other organisms. Spread by blood, CSF, or directly from nearby fractures of the frontal or facial bones.

## Findings
- Early: headache and fever.
- Positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, photophobia, nuchal (neck) rigidity, opisthotonus (arched back).

## Diagnosis
Lumbar puncture: culture and Gram stain of CSF and blood.

## Treatment
Large IV antibiotic doses (vancomycin, cephalosporins), dexamethasone, fluid expanders.

## Priority nursing actions
- Respiratory isolation for 24 hours after antibiotics start (protects others, first because it is infectious).
- Bed rest, dark quiet room, analgesics for headache.
- Frequent vital signs and neurologic checks.
- Fluid and electrolyte balance, daily weight; high-calorie, high-protein, small frequent meals.
- Prevent pressure injury and pneumonia.

## How the exam asks about it
Nuchal rigidity with fever and headache means meningitis; the isolation answer is droplet-type respiratory isolation for 24 hours after treatment begins.

## Related topics
[[Meningeal Signs, Babinski and Posturing]], [[Encephalitis]], [[Increased Intracranial Pressure]]

## Check against your textbook
Verify the precaution type and post-lumbar-puncture positioning, which the handout does not cover.

title: Encephalitis
body:
## What it is
Acute inflammation of brain tissue. Herpes simplex virus is most common; also fungi (Cryptococcus neoformans) and arthropod-borne viruses (carried by insects).

## Findings
Headache and fever (most common), nuchal rigidity, confusion, lowered consciousness, seizures, light sensitivity, ataxia, sleep changes, tremors, hemiparesis.

## Complications
Cognitive disability, personality change, motor deficits, blindness.

## Diagnosis
CT, MRI, lumbar puncture, EEG.

## Treatment
Anticonvulsants, antipyretics, analgesics, sedatives, and the antiviral acyclovir.

## Priority nursing actions
- Monitor vital signs and neurologic status often.
- Care for confused or unconscious client.
- Dim lights, reduce noise, give analgesics.
- Injury prevention is key: falls and seizures.

## How the exam asks about it
Tell it from meningitis: encephalitis affects thinking and behavior (confusion, personality change) while meningitis is dominated by meningeal signs.

## Related topics
[[Meningitis]], [[Seizure Nursing Care]], [[Neurologic Diagnostic Tests and Nursing Care]]

title: Seizure Types and Epilepsy
body:
## What it is
A seizure is a sudden abnormal burst of electrical discharge in the brain that changes movement, awareness or sensation. Epilepsy is a chronic disorder of repeated seizures.

## Causes
Idiopathic (genetic or developmental), brain injury, infection, vascular disease, drugs, poisons, drug or alcohol withdrawal, allergies.

## Classification
- Partial (focal): begins locally. Repetitive purposeless acts (lip smacking, picking at clothes).
  - Simple: no loss of consciousness; motor, sensory (hallucinations) or autonomic (flushing, fast pulse) signs; under 1 minute.
  - Complex (psychomotor): consciousness lost; 2 to 15 minutes.
- Generalized: whole cortex involved.
  - Absence (petit mal): brief staring spells, mostly children; triggered by stress, low sugar, fatigue, hyperventilation.
  - Tonic-clonic (grand mal): 30 to 60 seconds; rigidity, fixed dilated pupils, clenched hands and jaw, breathing may pause, urinary incontinence.
  - Clonic-type: repeated shock-like muscle jerks (handout writes "cyclonic").

## Status epilepticus
A series of grand mal seizures without waking in between: an emergency (handout: over 30 minutes).

## Diagnosis
EEG (most useful), CT, MRI.

## Related topics
[[Seizure Nursing Care]], [[Encephalitis]], [[Neurologic Diagnostic Tests and Nursing Care]]

## Check against your textbook
Modern definitions treat status epilepticus as about 5 minutes or more; "cyclonic" is probably myoclonic. Verify both.

title: Seizure Nursing Care
body:
## What it is
The nurse protects the client from injury and the airway from aspiration; never forces anything into the mouth.

## During a seizure
- Stay with the client, note the time.
- Ease the client to the floor; protect the head.
- Remove harmful objects; loosen tight clothing.
- Do not restrain. Do not place a tongue blade or insert an oral airway.
- Observe and record duration, body parts involved, and behaviors before and after.

## After the seizure
- Side-lying position to prevent aspiration.
- Suction equipment ready; bed in low position.
- Document events; reorient the client, allow rest.
- Check airway and breathing first, since aspiration is the main risk (ABC).

## How the exam asks about it
The wrong answers are usually "restrain the arms", "insert a tongue blade" or "give water". Pick the answer that protects the head and positions the client on their side.

## Related topics
[[Seizure Types and Epilepsy]], [[Encephalitis]], [[Increased Intracranial Pressure]]
outlineRefs: Nursing Management of seizures during and after

title: Myasthenia Gravis
body:
## What it is
A defect in impulse transmission at the nerve-muscle junction, with too little usable acetylcholine; cause unknown or autoimmune. Worse with activity, better with rest.

## Findings
Diplopia and ptosis (earliest), dysphonia, dysarthria, generalized weakness; respiratory paralysis is the cause of death.

## Diagnosis
- Edrophonium (Tensilon) test: fast-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; positive when facial weakness and ptosis clear within about 5 minutes. Atropine sulfate treats edrophonium toxicity.
- EMG shows delayed or failed neuromuscular transmission.

## Treatment
Pyridostigmine (first line), neostigmine, plasmapheresis, thymectomy.

## Drugs to avoid
Muscle relaxants, barbiturates, morphine, tranquilizers, neomycin.

## Priority nursing actions
- Airway first; watch breathing.
- Check gag reflex before feeding; semi-upright position; thick fluids; flex neck while eating; start with cold drinks.
- Give medicine 20 to 30 minutes before meals, on schedule.
- Protect from falls and infection; plan rest.

## Related topics
[[Myasthenic Crisis versus Cholinergic Crisis]], [[Neurons and Neurotransmitters]], [[Guillain-Barre Syndrome]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout blames increased acetylcholine destruction; textbooks describe antibodies against acetylcholine receptors. Verify.

title: Myasthenic Crisis versus Cholinergic Crisis
body:
## What it is
Two opposite emergencies in a client on anticholinesterase therapy.

## Myasthenic crisis
- Cause: undermedication (too little drug).
- Signs: severe weakness, higher blood pressure and heart rate, more secretions, breathing trouble.
- Handout intervention: give neostigmine (the drug that was missing).

## Cholinergic crisis
- Cause: overmedication.
- Signs: weakness with difficulty swallowing (the handout; cramps, salivation, slowed heart rate are also classic).
- Handout intervention: stop all cholinergic drugs.

## Priority actions
Both threaten breathing: check airway and breathing first, call for help, prepare for ventilation. Then identify which crisis, since the treatments are opposite.

## How the exam asks about it
Look at the clue: "missed dose" means myasthenic; "extra dose" means cholinergic. A short-acting edrophonium test separates them: improvement means myasthenic; worsening means cholinergic.

## Memory aid
Myasthenic = Missing drug; Cholinergic = Cause too much. Made-up helper.

## Related topics
[[Myasthenia Gravis]], [[Guillain-Barre Syndrome]]

## Check against your textbook
Atropine is the antidote for cholinergic crisis in most references; the handout lists only stopping the drug. Verify.

title: Multiple Sclerosis
body:
## What it is
A chronic, slowly progressive disease that strips the myelin from nerve fibers (demyelination), with periods of remission and exacerbation. Cause unknown; may follow a viral infection.

## Findings
- Charcot's triad: scanning speech, intention tremor, nystagmus.
- Vision: blurring, double vision, patchy or total blindness.
- Sensory: paresthesia, loss of position sense, pain.
- Cognitive: memory loss, poor concentration, dementia, poor abstract reasoning.
- Cerebellum and basal ganglia: ataxia, tremor, throat and face weakness.
- Others: bowel and bladder dysfunction, muscle hypertonicity.

## Diagnosis
MRI, CSF electrophoresis, EEG.

## Treatment
Interferon beta, methylprednisolone, other steroids, baclofen (drug of choice for spasticity).

## Nursing care
- Promote mobility: walking, assistive devices; swimming and stationary cycling ease spasticity.
- Avoid strenuous exercise (may trigger flare) and hot baths (burn risk because sensation is reduced).
- Prevent cuts and burns; eye patch for double vision; respiratory precautions; bowel and bladder program.

## How the exam asks about it
Pick "avoid overheating and fatigue". Fatigue and heat worsen symptoms.

## Related topics
[[Guillain-Barre Syndrome]], [[Trigeminal Neuralgia]], [[Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout lists "warm packs" for spasticity but also warns against hot baths; confirm. EEG as a test is questionable. Overheating avoidance is added knowledge.

title: Guillain-Barre Syndrome
body:
## What it is
An autoimmune attack on peripheral nerve myelin: rapid demyelination of peripheral and some cranial nerves. Weakness starts in the legs and ascends. More frequent in males. Cause unknown or after a viral infection.

## Findings
Clumsiness (initial), diminished reflexes, weakness moving upward, paresthesia, ataxia, dysphagia, eye muscle paralysis, diaphragm paralysis and respiratory depression.

## Complications
Respiratory failure, cardiac dysrhythmias, transient hypertension, orthostatic hypotension, pulmonary embolism.

## Diagnosis
EMG, CSF analysis, ECG.

## Treatment
Plasmapheresis; corticosteroids (handout).

## Priority nursing actions
- Breathing first: maintain ventilation, incentive spirometry, chest physiotherapy; watch for failure and prepare for ventilation.
- Monitor vital signs and heart rhythm; check cranial nerve function.
- Gag reflex before feeding; range-of-motion exercise.
- Care is mostly supportive; recovery is usually gradual.

## How the exam asks about it
"Ascending paralysis" means GBS; the first concern is respiratory function.

## Related topics
[[Myasthenia Gravis]], [[Multiple Sclerosis]], [[Respiratory Failure Recognition]]

## Check against your textbook
Corticosteroids are not shown to help in most references; immune globulin is the other standard treatment. Verify.

title: Parkinson's Disease: Signs and Pathophysiology
body:
## What it is
A slowly progressing movement disorder tied to low dopamine, eventually disabling.

## Pathophysiology
Dopamine-making cells in the substantia nigra die, so dopamine stores fall and the dopamine pathway degenerates. In the corpus striatum, acetylcholine (excitatory) outweighs dopamine (inhibiting), disturbing the extrapyramidal tracts that control complex movement.

## Causes
Usually idiopathic or degenerative; also viral infection, head trauma, antipsychotic drugs, free-radical buildup.

## Findings
- Cardinal signs: tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia (slow movement), postural instability.
- Others: pill-rolling, mask-like face, monotone speech, drooling, heavy sweating, festinating gait, gastric and urinary retention, micrographia (tiny writing), dysphonia.

## Diagnosis
Mostly clinical; PET and SPECT scans.

## How the exam asks about it
Pair "dopamine low" with levodopa treatment. Antipsychotic drugs (which block dopamine) can cause parkinson-like signs.

## Memory aid
TRAP: Tremor, Rigidity, Akinesia/bradykinesia, Postural instability. Widely used.

## Related topics
[[Parkinson's Disease: Drugs, Surgery and Nursing Care]], [[Neurons and Neurotransmitters]], [[Huntington's Disease]]

title: Parkinson's Disease: Drugs, Surgery and Nursing Care
body:
## What it is
Treatment replaces or imitates dopamine or blocks acetylcholine.

## Drugs
- Levodopa (most effective, mainstay), usually with carbidopa.
- Amantadine (antiviral).
- Dopamine agonists: bromocriptine, pergolide.
- Antihistamine: diphenhydramine (Benadryl).
- Anticholinergics: benztropine (Cogentin), trihexyphenidyl (Artane), Akineton.

## Surgery
Thalamotomy (common complications ataxia and hemiparesis), pallidotomy (destroying part of the globus pallidus in advanced disease), pacemaker-like brain implants.

## Levodopa teaching
- Side effects: nausea and vomiting, orthostatic hypotension, insomnia, agitation, confusion.
- Drugs that block its effect: phenothiazines, reserpine, vitamin B6 (pyridoxine).
- Handout foods to avoid (vitamin B6-rich): tuna, pork, dried beans, salmon, beef liver.

## Nursing care
- Mobility: walking, stationary bike, swimming, gardening; warm baths and massage.
- More fluid and fiber to prevent constipation.
- Aspiration precautions; semi-solid diet and thick fluids.
- Safety: orthostatic hypotension means rise slowly.

## Related topics
[[Parkinson's Disease: Signs and Pathophysiology]], [[Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma]]

## Check against your textbook
Vitamin B6 limits matter mainly for levodopa without carbidopa. "Renal damage" listed by the handout as a levodopa effect is doubtful. Anticholinergics raise eye pressure in glaucoma.

title: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
body:
## What it is
Lou Gehrig's disease: a progressive degeneration of motor neurons controlling voluntary muscles. Cause unknown; 5 to 10% inherited; too much of the transmitter glutamate is suspected.

## Findings
Fatigue, muscle weakness, cramps, fasciculations (twitching), dysphagia, breathing difficulty, inappropriate laughing or crying, constipation, urinary urgency.

## Diagnosis
EMG, muscle biopsy, MRI, EEG, CSF.

## Treatment
Riluzole (glutamate antagonist); baclofen, dantrolene or diazepam for spasticity; mechanical ventilation as respiratory muscles fail.

## Priority nursing actions
- Respiratory: keep airway clear, support gas exchange (oxygen, ventilatory assistance), prevent infection.
- Nutrition and swallowing safety.
- Maximize function: prevent immobility problems, self-care, communication aids, assistive devices.
- Support client and family.

## Related topics
[[Neurons and Neurotransmitters]], [[Multiple Sclerosis]], [[Guillain-Barre Syndrome]]

## Check against your textbook
Thinking and senses usually stay intact in ALS (added). EEG is an odd test here.

title: Spinal Cord Injury
body:
## What it is
Injury to the cord causing loss of sensation and movement below the level of damage. Causes: vehicle crashes, gunshots, falls, sports. Risk: young age, alcohol and drug use, male.

## Level of injury
- C1 to C4: respiratory depression (ventilator risk).
- C1 to C8: quadriplegia (some arm and hand movement at lower levels).
- T1 to T6: paraplegia, some trunk movement.
- T7 to T12: paraplegia, good upper back and abdominal strength.
- Lumbar, sacral, coccygeal: bowel, bladder and sexual dysfunction.

## Tests
X-ray, CT, MRI.

## Complications
Spinal and neurogenic shock, deep vein thrombosis, pressure ulcers, orthostatic hypotension, [[Autonomic Dysreflexia]].

## Priority nursing actions (and why)
- Breathing first, especially in cervical injury.
- Immobilize on flat, firm surface; cervical collar if neck injury suspected; move as a unit; do not realign body parts. Prevents further cord damage.
- Careful suctioning.
- Turn at least every 2 hours; intermittent catheterization for bladder distention.
- High-calorie, high-protein, high-fiber diet; fluids; bowel training.
- Anticoagulants and anti-embolism stockings against clots.

## Related topics
[[Primary vs Secondary Survey]], [[Spinal Nerves and the Autonomic Nervous System]], [[Types of Shock]]

title: Autonomic Dysreflexia
body:
## What it is
A life-threatening complication in clients with spinal injury at or above T6: a harmful stimulus below the injury triggers an uncontrolled sympathetic response the brain cannot balance.

## Triggers
Bladder distention (most common), bowel impaction, urinary tract infection, ingrown toenails, pressure ulcers.

## Findings
Pounding headache, profuse sweating, nasal congestion, goose bumps, bradycardia, blurred vision; severe hypertension is the danger (stroke risk).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Sit the client upright to lower blood pressure.
2. Find and remove the trigger: check the bladder (catheterize or unkink catheter) and check for fecal impaction.
3. Monitor blood pressure often.
4. If pressure stays high, antihypertensive such as hydralazine as ordered.

## How the exam asks about it
A quadriplegic client with a sudden severe headache and high pressure: raise the head and check the bladder first, before drugs.

## Related topics
[[Spinal Cord Injury]], [[Spinal Nerves and the Autonomic Nervous System]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout names hydralazine as the drug of choice; some references prefer fast-acting nifedipine or nitrates. Verify.

title: Alzheimer's Disease: Stages and Nursing Care
body:
## What it is
Progressive, irreversible degeneration of the brain, starting with gradual loss of thinking and changes in behavior and mood.

## Causes and brain changes
Unknown; possibly infection, Down syndrome (trisomy 21) in the 40s, and low acetylcholine activity in the cortex and hippocampus. Cortical atrophy, enlarged ventricles, amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles.

## Warning signs
Memory loss that affects work, difficulty with familiar tasks, language and abstract thinking problems, disorientation, mood and personality change.

## Stages
- Early: looks healthy; subtle personality change, forgetfulness, restlessness.
- Middle: memory deficit, may get lost, impaired language, cannot do daily activities, poor judgment, sundowning (more agitation and wandering in late day), cannot identify objects by touch, cannot write.
- Final: total dependence, loss of language and bowel and bladder control.

## Treatment
Cholinesterase inhibitors for mild to moderate disease (donepezil, rivastigmine, tacrine), memantine (NMDA antagonist); antidepressants, antipsychotics, anti-anxiety drugs for behavior.

## Nursing care
- Calm, predictable, familiar, noise-free environment; memory aids; clear short sentences.
- Safety: remove hazards, avoid restraints (they increase agitation), secure doors, ID bracelet.
- Simplify routines; encourage decisions; one dish at a time, small food pieces.

## Related topics
[[Alzheimer's Disease]], [[Delirium versus Dementia]], [[Neurons and Neurotransmitters]]

## Check against your textbook
Brain biopsy is listed as confirmatory, but diagnosis is clinical with confirmation after death. Tacrine is rarely used because of liver toxicity. Cholinesterase inhibitors work by preventing breakdown of acetylcholine.

title: Bell's Palsy
body:
## What it is
One-sided inflammation of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) causing facial weakness and paralysis with rapid onset. Adults under 45; both sexes. Cause unknown; autoimmune, viral (herpes simplex or zoster) or bacterial.

## Pathophysiology
Inflamed, swollen nerve gets squeezed, blood supply is blocked and the nerve is damaged (ischemic necrosis).

## Findings
Cannot close the eye fully on that side, ptosis, ear or jaw pain, one-sided weakness, ringing in the ear, difficulty eating, loss of taste on the front of the tongue, flattened nasolabial fold.

## Diagnosis
History and physical, EMG.

## Treatment
Prednisone (7 to 10 days), analgesics, antivirals; heat, gentle massage, electrical nerve stimulation.

## Nursing care
- Soft diet; chew on the unaffected side; avoid hot food and drink (reduced sensation).
- Artificial tears to protect the cornea.
- Facial exercises: grimacing, wrinkling, whistling, puffing cheeks.
- Reassure: usually improves.

## How the exam asks about it
Do not confuse with stroke: Bell's palsy affects the whole side of the face, including forehead.

## Related topics
[[Cranial Nerves: Names, Types and Functions]], [[Trigeminal Neuralgia]], [[Stroke: Deficits and Left versus Right Hemisphere]]

## Check against your textbook
Stroke-versus-Bell's forehead sparing and eye-patching at night are added general knowledge.

title: Huntington's Disease
body:
## What it is
Inherited, progressive wasting of the basal ganglia and parts of the cortex. Appears at about 25 to 55 years. Autosomal inheritance; rate about 1 in 10,000 (handout text is garbled).

## Pathophysiology
Degeneration of the corpus striatum and caudate nucleus leads to loss of normal movement and intellect.

## Findings
Chorea (jerky involuntary movements), dystonic posture, dysarthria, hesitant speech and eye blinking, impaired chewing and swallowing, progressive cognitive decline, personality change, depression, psychosis.

## Diagnosis
History and physical, MRI, CT, genetic testing.

## Treatment
Thiothixene or haloperidol for chorea; levodopa for rigidity (per handout).

## Nursing care
- Foster independence in daily activities; assistive devices.
- Aspiration precautions; soft foods.
- Calm but firm directions; safe environment.
- Support groups and genetic counseling.

## Related topics
[[Parkinson's Disease: Signs and Pathophysiology]], [[Alzheimer's Disease: Stages and Nursing Care]]

## Check against your textbook
Huntington's is autosomal dominant. Levodopa can worsen chorea; verify the rigidity statement.

title: Trigeminal Neuralgia
body:
## What it is
Tic douloureux: sudden attacks of one-sided facial pain along the branches of cranial nerve V (second and third branches most common). Linked to multiple sclerosis.

## Causes
Chronic nerve compression or irritation, degeneration of the Gasserian ganglion, blood vessels pressing on the nerve.

## Findings
Intense jabbing, burning or knife-like pain that begins and ends suddenly and lasts seconds to minutes.

## Diagnosis
History, observation of an attack, CT, MRI.

## Treatment
- Anti-seizure drugs: carbamazepine, phenytoin; alcohol or phenol injection.
- Surgery: microvascular decompression, radiofrequency thermal coagulation, percutaneous balloon microcompression.

## Nursing care
- Prevent triggers: very hot or cold food, jarring the bed, washing face, combing hair, brushing teeth.
- Use cotton pads and room-temperature water; rinse mouth after eating; chew on the unaffected side; soft foods.
- After surgery: sensory loss means do not rub the eye, check for redness, use artificial tears.

## Related topics
[[Bell's Palsy]], [[Multiple Sclerosis]], [[Cranial Nerves: Names, Types and Functions]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout says trigeminal neuralgia is 400 times more common in MS; confirm this figure.

title: Eye Anatomy
body:
## What it is
Parts of the eye and what each does.

## Structures
- Cornea: clear, blood-vessel-free dome; main refracting surface.
- Aqueous humor: made by the ciliary body; nourishes the cornea.
- Uvea: iris, ciliary body and choroid.
- Iris: the colored part. Pupil: opening that widens and narrows with light.
- Lens: clear, biconvex; focuses near and far (accommodation).
- Choroid: blood vessel layer feeding the outer retina.
- Vitreous humor: fills about two-thirds of the eye and keeps its shape.
- Retina: neural tissue, an extension of the optic nerve. The macula gives central vision. Rods: night vision. Cones: bright light and color.

## How the exam asks about it
Link structure to disease: lens clouding is cataract; blocked outflow of aqueous humor is glaucoma; macula damage is central vision loss; detached retina is a floaters-and-curtain emergency.

## Memory aid
Rods = "rod, dark"; cones = "color". Made-up helper.

## Related topics
[[Cataract]], [[Chronic Open-Angle Glaucoma]], [[Retinal Detachment]], [[Macular Degeneration]]

title: Vision Tests and Eye Examination Tools
body:
## What it is
Common eye tests and what each measures.

## Tests
- Snellen chart: distance vision. 20/20 is normal. 20/200 means you see at 20 feet what a normal eye sees at 200 feet.
- Ophthalmoscope: fundus, optic cup, retina periphery, macula.
- Slit lamp: binocular microscope magnifying 10 to 40 times.
- Tonometer: measures eye pressure by flattening a small area of the cornea. Normal intraocular pressure (IOP) is 10 to 21 mm Hg.
- Perimetry: visual field testing.
- Ishihara plates: color blindness; colored dots form numbers or shapes.
- Amsler grid: for macular problems; patient fixes on the central spot, and faded squares or wavy lines indicate trouble.

## How the exam asks about it
Match the test to the disease: tonometry for glaucoma, Amsler for macular degeneration, slit lamp for cataract, fluorescein for corneal abrasion.

## Related topics
[[Macular Degeneration]], [[Chronic Open-Angle Glaucoma]], [[Cataract]], [[Corneal Abrasion and Keratitis]]

title: Eye Terms and Eye Removal Surgeries
body:
## What it is
Vocabulary that exam items assume you know.

## Terms
- Aphakia: no lens. Emmetropia: normal vision.
- Hyperopia: farsighted. Myopia: nearsighted. Astigmatism: uneven corneal curve.
- Diplopia: double vision. Strabismus: eyes not aligned. Nystagmus: involuntary eye oscillation.
- Ptosis: drooping eyelid. Hyperemia: red eye. Papilledema: swelling of the optic disc.
- Proptosis: eyeball bulging forward.
- Blindness and legal blindness: legal blindness is best corrected acuity of 20/200 or worse.

## Eye removal surgery
- Enucleation: removes the whole eyeball and part of the optic nerve.
- Evisceration: removes the contents of the eye through the cornea or sclera, leaving the shell.
- Exenteration: removes eyelids, eye and varying amounts of the orbit contents.

## Related topics
[[Penetrating Eye Injuries and Splash Injuries]], [[Eye Anatomy]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout defines proptosis as downward displacement and lists blindness as "20/400"; textbooks say forward protrusion and describe blindness differently. Verify.

title: Blepharitis, Stye and Chalazion
body:
## What it is
Eyelid inflammations, usually from Staphylococcus aureus.

## Blepharitis
Inflammation of the lid margin. Findings: flaking, redness, irritation, recurrent styes. Treatment: antibiotic ointment to lid margin 1 to 4 times daily if staph is likely. Teach: scrub lid margin with cotton swab and apply ointment with a swab.

## Hordeolum (stye) and chalazion
- Stye: infection of lid glands or follicles; external stye involves the eyelash follicles.
- Chalazion: chronic granuloma of the meibomian glands.
- Findings: pain, redness, foreign body feeling, pustule.
- Treatment: warm soaks for drainage, hand washing and lid hygiene, antibiotic ointment; sometimes incision and drainage.

## Client teaching
Never squeeze a stye; clean lid margins; wash hands.

## Related topics
[[Conjunctivitis]], [[Eye Anatomy]]

title: Conjunctivitis
body:
## What it is
Inflammation of the conjunctiva, the membrane over the sclera and inside the lids. "Pink eye" usually means infectious conjunctivitis.

## Types
- Bacterial: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus.
- Viral: adenovirus, herpes simplex.
- Allergic: hay fever or pollen.

## Findings
Foreign body feeling, burning, itching, light sensitivity.

## Nursing care
- Bacterial: warm soaks 10 minutes four times daily to remove crusting; broad-spectrum antibiotic drops (teach instillation).
- Viral: cold compress.
- Allergic: antihistamines, vasoconstrictors, mast cell stabilizers.
- Hand washing to stop spread; avoid touching eyes (standard teaching, not in handout).

## How the exam asks about it
Infection control: it is contagious, so prevent spread within the family and school.

## Related topics
[[Blepharitis, Stye and Chalazion]], [[Corneal Abrasion and Keratitis]]

title: Corneal Abrasion and Keratitis
body:
## What it is
Loss of the surface layer of the cornea from injury (fingernail, branch, spark, overwearing contact lenses). It can become an ulcer and infected (keratitis), possibly causing blindness.

## Findings
Pain, redness, foreign body feeling, light sensitivity, tearing, trouble opening the eye.

## Diagnosis
Fluorescein stain with Wood's lamp or slit lamp.

## Treatment
- Urgent. Strong antibiotic drops and eye patch for 24 hours; cycloplegics to relieve ciliary spasm pain.
- Abrasion heals in 24 to 48 hours; ulcer needs an ophthalmologist.
- Make sure the patch holds the lid closed.
- After the patch: topical antibiotic (or antiviral for herpes simplex dendritic keratitis).

## Teaching
Wear protective eye shields; wash hands often; follow up.

## Related topics
[[Conjunctivitis]], [[Uveitis (Iritis)]], [[Vision Tests and Eye Examination Tools]]

title: Uveitis (Iritis)
body:
## What it is
Inflammation inside the eye. Anterior uveitis (iris or iris and ciliary body) is most common and usually one-sided. Intermediate involves structures behind the lens. Posterior involves choroid, retina or vitreous and is usually both eyes.

## Causes
Immune-mediated disease, idiopathic, ankylosing spondylitis, Crohn's disease, Reiter's syndrome, lupus, trauma.

## Findings
Sudden deep eye pain, light sensitivity, red conjunctiva, small pupil that reacts sluggishly.

## Treatment and care
- Urgent ophthalmology review.
- Topical corticosteroid plus a cycloplegic.
- Teach drop technique and strict schedule to prevent permanent damage.
- Sunglasses for light sensitivity.
- Follow-up IOP checks because steroids can raise eye pressure.

## How the exam asks about it
Compare pupils: uveitis has a small pupil; acute glaucoma has a mid-dilated, fixed pupil.

## Related topics
[[Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma]], [[Corneal Abrasion and Keratitis]]

title: Cataract
body:
## What it is
Clouding of the lens that blocks vision.

## Types and risks
Senile (age), congenital, traumatic. Risk: diabetes, ultraviolet light, radiation, corticosteroids, phenothiazines, some chemotherapy.

## Findings
Blurred or distorted vision, glare, slow painless loss of vision, a pupil that looks milky or white.

## Diagnosis
Slit lamp, ophthalmoscopy to rule out retinal disease, perimetry (fields normal), Snellen test.

## Treatment
Surgical removal of the lens, usually under local anesthesia. Eye drops before surgery for pain control and less movement; oral drugs may lower IOP. Lens implant (IOL) at the time of surgery.

## Related topics
[[Cataract Surgery and Lens Replacement]], [[Vision Tests and Eye Examination Tools]], [[Eye Anatomy]]

title: Cataract Surgery and Lens Replacement
body:
## What it is
Surgical techniques and care for cataract extraction.

## Techniques
- Intracapsular: lens and capsule removed.
- Extracapsular: capsule opened, nucleus and cortex removed, posterior capsule left to hold an implant.
- Cryosurgery: supercooled probe (about -35 degrees C) freezes the lens for removal.
- Phacoemulsification: ultrasound liquefies the lens, then it is suctioned out.

## Lens replacement
Aphakic glasses (objects look 25% bigger and closer), contact lenses, intraocular lens implants (usual choice: monofocal, multifocal, accommodative).

## Before surgery
Orient and explain; do not touch the eyes; ordered drops (antibiotic, mydriatic-cycloplegic), sedative, antiemetic.

## After surgery
- Prevent rise in eye pressure: no coughing, sneezing, rapid movement or bending from the waist; head up 30 degrees, lie on the unaffected side.
- Report sudden pain with restlessness and fast pulse (pressure) or fever (infection).
- Pain and nausea control; wear glasses or metal shield as instructed.
- Wipe the closed eye from the inner corner outward with clean tissue.
- Help the client move around safely with one eye patched for 1 to 2 days.

## Related topics
[[Cataract]], [[Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma]]

title: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma
body:
## What it is
Blocked fluid outflow at the drainage angle causes severely high pressure. An eye emergency that can cause blindness quickly.

## Findings
Eye pain, red congested eye, nausea and vomiting, slow pulse, sweating, peripheral vision loss, very high IOP, corneal swelling, pupil oval, fixed and semi-dilated.

## Diagnosis
Tonometry, ophthalmoscopy, gonioscopy, perimetry.

## Treatment
- Acetazolamide (Diamox) to lower pressure by diuresis; pilocarpine (constricts pupil) and beta-blocker drops.
- Laser iridotomy; the other eye is also treated to prevent an attack.

## Teaching
Long-term drops; follow-up; return at once for severe pain, light sensitivity, heavy tearing; avoid corticosteroids and anticholinergics (e.g. Akineton, diphenhydramine, benztropine).

## How the exam asks about it
Sudden severe eye pain with halos and vomiting equals an emergency; priority is rapid pressure reduction, not pain medicine alone.

## Related topics
[[Chronic Open-Angle Glaucoma]], [[Uveitis (Iritis)]], [[Parkinson's Disease: Drugs, Surgery and Nursing Care]]

## Check against your textbook
Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, not a hyperosmotic agent as the handout says.

title: Chronic Open-Angle Glaucoma
body:
## What it is
Slowly rising eye pressure damages the optic nerve and visual fields. About 90% of primary glaucoma; rises with age; usually both eyes. The angle looks normal.

## Findings
Mild tired or foggy eyes, slow peripheral vision loss while central vision stays (tunnel vision), halos around lights, optic disc cupping.

## Diagnosis
Tonometry, optic disc exam, visual field tests.

## Treatment
- Miotic drops widen outflow; oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and beta blockers reduce production.
- Laser trabeculoplasty if drugs fail.

## Nursing care
- Painless but progressive: lifelong drops and follow-up even without symptoms.
- Avoid straining, heavy lifting, bending.
- Low-sodium diet (per handout).
- Explain actions, doses and adverse effects of all eye medicines.

## Related topics
[[Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma]], [[Vision Tests and Eye Examination Tools]]

## Check against your textbook
Low-sodium diet for glaucoma is questionable; verify.

title: Retinal Detachment
body:
## What it is
The sensory retina (rods and cones) separates from the pigment layer under it, often after holes or tears, trauma, inflammation or tumor.

## Findings
Floaters, flashes of light, blank areas of vision, a veil or curtain. If untreated: loss of central and side vision, legal blindness.

## Diagnosis
Indirect ophthalmoscopy (gray retina), slit lamp, ultrasound or optical coherence tomography.

## Surgery
Scleral buckling (band indents the eye wall), pneumatic retinopexy (gas bubble or oil pushes the retina back), cryopexy (freezing probe makes a scar that seals it).

## After surgery
- Avoid bumping the head, coughing, sneezing, straining and bending head below the waist; avoid rapid eye movements for weeks.
- Pain and nausea control; encourage safe activity; diversion such as radio.
- Driving restricted; light activity at 3 weeks, heavier activity at 6 weeks.
- Warm moist washcloth for comfort; clean technique for eye drops.
- Report new floaters, flashes or shadows. First follow-up at 2 weeks.

## Related topics
[[Macular Degeneration]], [[Cataract Surgery and Lens Replacement]]

## Check against your textbook
Post-gas-bubble positioning (often a specific head position) is not given; also avoid air travel and altitude after a gas bubble. Verify.

title: Macular Degeneration
body:
## What it is
The leading cause of vision loss over 60: damage to the macula, causing loss of central vision while side vision remains.

## Types
- Dry (nonexudative): slow breakdown of outer retina; drusen deposits; gradual blurring, noticed while reading. No cure.
- Wet (exudative): abnormal vessels grow under the retina and leak; sudden onset; straight lines look wavy or letters look broken.

## Treatment
- Dry: antioxidants (vitamins C, E, beta-carotene) and zinc may slow progression in high-risk people.
- Wet: ranibizumab (Lucentis) or bevacizumab (Avastin).

## Nursing care
Teach the Amsler grid at home: look at it one eye at a time, with glasses on, several times a week. Report any change at once.

## Related topics
[[Vision Tests and Eye Examination Tools]], [[Retinal Detachment]]

## Check against your textbook
"Megadoses" is the handout's wording; use doses from a reference.

title: Orbital Trauma and Fractures
body:
## What it is
Injury to the eye socket, often with head injury.

## Priority
Stabilize the general condition first (airway, breathing, circulation), then examine the eye. Suspect facial fractures in any blunt trauma. A soft globe, prolapsed tissue, ruptured globe or bleeding needs immediate surgery.

## Soft tissue injury
- Findings: tenderness, bruising, lid swelling, proptosis, "black eye" with subconjunctival bleeding; optic nerve damage possible.
- Care: cold compresses early, warm later; drain large hematomas; steroids reduce optic nerve swelling; decompression if needed.

## Orbital fracture
- Types: blowout, zygomatic (tripod), maxillary, midfacial, orbital apex, orbital roof.
- Findings: entrapped muscle or nerve, globe sinking in (enophthalmos); caused by a blunt object (fist, ball).
- CT shows entrapment. Orbital roof fractures are dangerous because of brain involvement. Emergency repair if the globe is pushed into the sinus.

## Related topics
[[Penetrating Eye Injuries and Splash Injuries]], [[Primary vs Secondary Survey]]

title: Penetrating Eye Injuries and Splash Injuries
body:
## What it is
Wounds that pierce or bruise the globe, and splashes of chemicals.

## Findings
Marked vision loss, chemosis, conjunctival tear, shallow anterior chamber with distorted pupil, hyphema (blood in front chamber), vitreous hemorrhage.

## First aid for penetrating injury
- Do not try to remove the object; keep it from moving.
- No pressure and no patch on the eye.
- Protect with a metal shield or a stiff paper cup until treatment.
- Prevent bleeding and rising pressure.

## Treatment
Topical steroids, aminocaproic acid for clots, tetanus protection, antibiotics. If the eye cannot be repaired and has no light perception, enucleation within about 2 weeks prevents sympathetic ophthalmia (inflammation damaging the good eye).

## Splash injury
Irrigate immediately with tap water or saline. Avoid manipulating a ruptured globe; defer cycloplegics and topical drops in that case.

## How the exam asks about it
Penetrating object: shield, do not remove, do not patch. Chemical splash: irrigate first.

## Related topics
[[Orbital Trauma and Fractures]], [[Eye Terms and Eye Removal Surgeries]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout mixes irrigation (for chemicals) with ruptured-globe precautions; do not irrigate a ruptured globe.
outlineRefs: Penetrating Injuries and Contusion of the Eyeball

title: Ear Anatomy
body:
## What it is
The ear has three parts for hearing, and the inner ear also handles balance.

## Parts
- External ear: auricle collects sound; ear canal about 2.5 cm long, with hair, oil glands and wax (cerumen) glands.
- Middle ear: tympanic membrane (eardrum), about 1 cm, normally pearly gray and translucent; conducts vibrations to the ossicles: malleus, incus, stapes (the smallest bones in the body).
- Inner ear: in the temporal bone. Cochlea (hearing) and semicircular canals (balance), in the bony labyrinth filled with perilymph. Organ of Corti in the cochlea turns vibrations into nerve signals and separates frequencies. Cochlear and vestibular nerves join to form cranial nerve VIII.

## How the exam asks about it
Locate a disease: otitis externa is in the canal, otitis media behind the drum, Meniere's in the inner ear.

## Related topics
[[Hearing Tests: Weber, Rinne and Audiometry]], [[Otitis Externa]], [[Meniere's Disease]], [[Cranial Nerves: Names, Types and Functions]]

title: Hearing Tests: Weber, Rinne and Audiometry
body:
## What it is
Examining the ear and testing hearing.

## Inspection
Check the auricle for deformity, lesions, discharge, size and symmetry. Pain on moving the auricle suggests external otitis; mastoid tenderness suggests mastoiditis; flaky scaling suggests seborrheic dermatitis.

## Tools
- Otoscope: views the canal and drum.
- Whisper test: cover one ear, whisper 1 to 2 feet away; a normal person repeats it.
- Weber: tuning fork on the forehead; tests which ear hears bone-conducted sound better.
- Rinne: compares air conduction (fork near the ear) and bone conduction (fork on mastoid).
- Audiometry: pure-tone (louder needed means more loss) and speech.

## Interpreting
- Normal: Weber equal in both ears; Rinne air louder than bone.
- Conductive loss: Weber louder in the affected ear; Rinne bone longer than air.
- Sensorineural loss: Weber louder in the better ear; Rinne air longer than bone.

## Memory aid
Conductive = "Weber toward the bad ear"; sensorineural = "away from it". Made-up helper.

## Related topics
[[Ear Anatomy]], [[Otosclerosis and Stapedectomy]], [[Meniere's Disease]], [[Cranial Nerve Testing and Deficits]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout says to hold the otoscope in the right hand; technique varies (adult ear: pull up and back). Verify.

title: Otitis Externa
body:
## What it is
Inflammation of the ear canal (swimmer's ear).

## Causes
Bacteria (Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus aureus), fungi (Aspergillus, Candida), trauma from cleaning, water trapped after swimming.

## Findings
Pain, discharge (yellow or green, foul), tenderness, fever, swollen glands, fullness or hearing loss, red swollen canal; black spore threads in fungal infection.

## Treatment
- Antibiotic drops with corticosteroid; a wick if the canal is swollen shut.
- Burow's solution or steroid cream for dermatitis; nystatin for fungal.
- Clean debris after pain eases; warm compresses and analgesics.

## Teaching
Do not clean the canal with cotton swabs; keep it dry during swimming and shampooing; use antiseptic ear drops after swimming.

## Related topics
[[Acute Otitis Media]], [[Impacted Cerumen and Ear Foreign Bodies]], [[Ear Anatomy]]

title: Acute Otitis Media
body:
## What it is
Infection of the middle ear with rapid onset, common in children but possible at any age. Germs enter through a poorly working eustachian tube.

## Organisms
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus.

## Findings
One or both ears; progressive conductive or mixed hearing loss; may have tinnitus; the drum may look normal or pinkish-orange.

## Related care
Treatment is usually an antibiotic with pain and fever relief. Untreated infection can spread (mastoiditis) or cause lasting hearing loss.

## Related topics
[[Otitis Externa]], [[Hearing Tests: Weber, Rinne and Audiometry]], [[Otosclerosis and Stapedectomy]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's description (bone conduction better than air; normal drum; stapedectomy) fits otosclerosis, not acute otitis media. The usual findings (ear pain, fever, red bulging drum) and antibiotic treatment are added from general knowledge. Verify.

title: Otosclerosis and Stapedectomy
body:
## What it is
In otosclerosis the stapes becomes fixed, causing slowly worsening conductive hearing loss. Stapedectomy removes the stapes (or its upper part and part of the footplate) and replaces it with a tissue graft and prosthesis.

## Findings
Progressive conductive loss, possible tinnitus, normal-looking drum, bone conduction better than air on Rinne.

## After surgery
- Balance disturbance or true vertigo may last several days, so protect from falls.
- Standard care (not from handout): avoid blowing the nose hard, sneezing with mouth closed, straining, flying and loud noises; report severe dizziness, sudden hearing loss or drainage.

## How the exam asks about it
Conductive hearing loss with a normal drum and Rinne bone better than air.

## Related topics
[[Hearing Tests: Weber, Rinne and Audiometry]], [[Acute Otitis Media]], [[Ear Anatomy]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout gives the surgery under the "otitis media" heading; confirm the condition and the activity restrictions with your textbook.

title: Meniere's Disease
body:
## What it is
Abnormal inner-ear fluid balance (endolymph).

## Findings
- Meniere's triad: tinnitus (roaring), vertigo with nausea and vomiting, sensorineural hearing loss.
- Fluctuating hearing loss and ear fullness.

## Diagnosis
Caloric testing (can bring on an attack); audiogram shows sensorineural loss; CT or MRI to exclude acoustic neuroma.

## Treatment
- Diary of attacks.
- Diuretics (acetazolamide, per handout); vestibular suppressants: meclizine (up to 25 mg four times a day), diphenhydramine 25 to 50 mg three to four times a day, diazepam (habit-forming); promethazine for nausea.
- Gentamicin or streptomycin to destroy vestibular function if vertigo is uncontrollable.
- Surgery: endolymphatic sac decompression; labyrinthectomy (total deafness in that ear); vestibular nerve section.

## Complications
Irreversible hearing loss, social isolation, falls.

## Nursing care
- During an attack: lie still in a safe place (fall prevention).
- Low salt and sugar; limit alcohol; avoid aspirin.
- Teach medicines and side effects; keep a log of attacks and triggers; hearing follow-up.

## Related topics
[[Hearing Tests: Weber, Rinne and Audiometry]], [[Ear Anatomy]]

## Check against your textbook
Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, not an osmotic diuretic. Confirm the doses listed.

title: Impacted Cerumen and Ear Foreign Bodies
body:
## What it is
Ear wax packed in the canal, or objects and insects in the ear. Wax is drier in older people; cotton swabs push it deeper; children insert beans, beads, toys.

## Findings
Reduced hearing, plugged feeling, pain, fever, drainage; an insect may cause a low rumbling.

## Management of cerumen
- Irrigate (not with a perforated drum or inflamed canal); direct the stream behind the wax.
- Soften first with warm glycerin, mineral oil or half-strength peroxide for about 30 minutes.
- Curette, suction or microscope if needed.

## Foreign objects
- Insects: put in mineral oil.
- Do not irrigate where this could swell or push the object (handout says irrigation is contraindicated for insects).
- Mechanical removal or suction; general anesthesia may be needed.

## Related topics
[[Otitis Externa]], [[Ear Anatomy]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout wording on irrigation is unclear; usual rule is no irrigation for vegetable matter or with a perforated eardrum.
